learnings.title: F.prototype vs f.__proto__
learnings.answer:
The short answer: **`F.prototype` and `f.__proto__` point to the same object**, but they live on different things and serve different roles.

If `F` is a constructor function and `f` is an instance created with `new F()`:

```javascript
f.__proto__ === F.prototype; // true
```

## `F.prototype` — the blueprint

The `.prototype` property exists **only on functions**. When you define a function, the engine attaches a `.prototype` object to it. That object is the shared blueprint for every instance created with `new F()`.

- **Lives on:** the constructor function (`F`)
- **Purpose:** holds methods and properties shared by all instances of `F`
- **Created when:** the function `F` is defined

```javascript
function Animal(name) {
  this.name = name;
}

Animal.prototype.speak = function () {
  console.log(this.name + " makes a noise.");
};
```

## `f.__proto__` — the link

`.__proto__` is an accessor on almost every object. It points to the prototype object that **this specific instance** inherits from — the spec's internal `[[Prototype]]` link.

When you access `f.speak()`, JavaScript looks on `f` first. If the property isn't there, it follows `f.__proto__` (i.e. `F.prototype`) to find shared methods.

- **Lives on:** the instance object (`f`)
- **Purpose:** the actual inheritance link from instance → constructor blueprint
- **Created when:** the object `f` is instantiated with `new`

```javascript
const myDog = new Animal("Rex");

myDog.speak(); // "Rex makes a noise."

console.log(myDog.__proto__ === Animal.prototype); // true
```

> `__proto__` is legacy. Prefer **`Object.getPrototypeOf(f)`** for reading the link.

```javascript
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(myDog) === Animal.prototype); // true
```

## Summary comparison

| Feature | `F.prototype` | `f.__proto__` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Where does it live?** | On the constructor function | On the instance object |
| **What is its job?** | Blueprint for new instances | Pointer to that blueprint |
| **When is it created?** | When `F` is defined | When `f` is instantiated |
| **Modern standard** | Standard and actively used | Legacy — use `Object.getPrototypeOf()` |

## Mental model

```
F (constructor)          f (instance)
    │                        │
    └── .prototype ◄─────────┴── .__proto__  (same object)
              │
         shared methods
```

One object, two views: the constructor **defines** the blueprint (`F.prototype`); each instance **references** it (`f.__proto__` / `[[Prototype]]`).

learnings.title: Parallelism vs Concurrency
learnings.answer:
The distinction between **concurrency** and **parallelism** comes down to **structure** versus **physical execution**.

Rob Pike put it simply:

> **Concurrency** is about dealing with a lot of things at once. **Parallelism** is about doing a lot of things at once.

- **Concurrency** is a way to **structure** a program — breaking it into independent tasks that can make progress over overlapping time periods.
- **Parallelism** is a way to **execute** a program — running those tasks at the exact same moment across multiple processing units.

## The kitchen analogy

**Concurrency (one cook):** You put rice on to boil, switch to chopping vegetables, then check the oven. You are making progress on multiple dishes, but at any exact moment your hands are only doing one specific task.

**Parallelism (multiple cooks):** You hire two more cooks. One boils rice, one chops vegetables, one mans the oven. All three tasks happen at the same physical time.

## Concurrency: managing overlapping tasks

Concurrency happens when tasks **start, run, and complete in overlapping time periods**. It does not mean they run at the exact same microsecond — the system rapidly switches context between them so they all make progress.

### Frontend (JavaScript)

When building UIs with JavaScript, TypeScript, React, or Vue, you operate in a **concurrent but single-threaded** world. The browser's JavaScript engine has one call stack.

If a component fetches data from an API, the main thread cannot freeze while waiting — the whole UI would lock up. Instead, the runtime offloads the network request to the environment and immediately continues rendering or handling events. The **event loop** is what makes this juggling possible.

```javascript
// Concurrent, not parallel — one thread, overlapping work
async function loadUser() {
  const res = await fetch("/api/user"); // main thread is free while waiting
  const user = await res.json();
  setUser(user); // UI updates when data arrives
}
```

### Backend (async I/O)

On a backend built with FastAPI (or Node.js), `async`/`await` lets a **single worker** handle thousands of database queries. While waiting for PostgreSQL to return data for User A, the server switches to processing User B. Highly concurrent — maximizing I/O efficiency without needing multiple CPU cores.

## Parallelism: simultaneous execution

Parallelism requires **physical hardware** — multiple CPU cores or separate machines. It is the literal simultaneous execution of multiple computations.

### Frontend (Web Workers)

For a **CPU-bound** task on the frontend — parsing a massive dataset, image processing — standard JavaScript concurrency will not help; the main thread still blocks. To achieve parallelism, spin up **Web Workers**, distributing work to separate threads on different CPU cores.

```javascript
// main thread
const worker = new Worker("parse-worker.js");
worker.postMessage(largeDataset);
worker.onmessage = (e) => console.log("Parsed:", e.data);
```

See also **Web Workers (#133)** in this app for API details and limitations.

### Backend (multi-process / multi-core)

Deploying a Dockerized app on a multi-core AWS instance lets you run multiple worker processes (e.g. Uvicorn workers). If four users hit the server at once, four separate CPU cores can process Python code for each user **simultaneously**.

## Summary comparison

| Feature | Concurrency | Parallelism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Core concept** | Juggling multiple tasks | Executing tasks simultaneously |
| **Focus** | Program structure & design | Hardware execution |
| **Hardware** | Can run on a single-core CPU | Requires multi-core or multiple CPUs |
| **Best for** | I/O-bound work (network, DB queries) | CPU-bound work (image processing, heavy math) |
| **Bottleneck** | Waiting on external resources | CPU processing power |
| **JS example** | `fetch` + event loop, `async`/`await` | Web Workers |

## Interview one-liner

> "JavaScript in the browser is **concurrent** by design — one thread juggling async I/O via the event loop. **Parallelism** needs extra threads (Web Workers) or multiple processes on the server. Concurrency is how you organize work; parallelism is how many cores actually run it at once."

learnings.title: Event Propagation: Bubbling, Capturing, and the Three Phases
learnings.answer:
**Question:** explain event propagation. What are bubbling and capturing, how do they differ, and how do you implement both?

## The three phases

When you click an element, the event doesn't fire only there. It travels through the DOM in three phases:

1. **Capturing** — from `window` *down* to the target
2. **Target** — at the clicked element itself
3. **Bubbling** — from the target back *up* to `window`

```
          CAPTURING ↓            ↑ BUBBLING
          window                 window
            document               document
              body                   body
                div                    div
                  button  ←— TARGET —→  button
```

Every ancestor gets two chances to hear about the event: once on the way down, once on the way back up.

## Implementing both

The third argument to `addEventListener` chooses the phase:

```javascript
// Bubbling — the default
parent.addEventListener('click', handler);
parent.addEventListener('click', handler, false);

// Capturing
parent.addEventListener('click', handler, true);
parent.addEventListener('click', handler, { capture: true });
```

Only **ancestors** are affected by the flag. A listener on the target itself fires in the target phase regardless, in the order the listeners were registered.

## The difference in one line

Bubbling runs **innermost first**; capturing runs **outermost first**.

```javascript
document.querySelector('.outer')
  .addEventListener('click', () => console.log('outer capture'), true);
document.querySelector('.inner')
  .addEventListener('click', () => console.log('inner capture'), true);
document.querySelector('.inner')
  .addEventListener('click', () => console.log('inner bubble'));
document.querySelector('.outer')
  .addEventListener('click', () => console.log('outer bubble'));

// Clicking .inner logs:
// outer capture   ← down
// inner capture
// inner bubble    ← target, then up
// outer bubble
```

## Useful properties

| Property / method | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `event.target` | Where the event actually originated — **doesn't change** as it propagates |
| `event.currentTarget` | The element whose listener is running right now |
| `event.eventPhase` | `1` capturing, `2` target, `3` bubbling |
| `event.stopPropagation()` | Stop travelling further along the path |
| `event.stopImmediatePropagation()` | Also skip other listeners on this same element |
| `event.preventDefault()` | Cancel the default action; propagation continues |

The `target` vs `currentTarget` distinction is what makes [event delegation](/learnings/152) possible.

## When capturing is actually useful

Bubbling is the default because it's what you want almost always. Capturing earns its place when you need to act **before** anything downstream can:

- Intercepting or blocking an event before a child's handler sees it
- Analytics that must record every click even if a child stops propagation
- A modal or overlay that swallows interaction with the page behind it

## Events that don't bubble

Not everything bubbles: `focus`, `blur`, `load`, `mouseenter`, `mouseleave`. Use the bubbling equivalents when you need delegation — `focusin`/`focusout` for focus, and `mouseover`/`mouseout` for hover.

## Related

- [Nested Click Handlers: Execution Order](/learnings/147)
- [Event Delegation](/learnings/152)
- [preventDefault vs stopPropagation](/learnings/97)

learnings.title: Nested Click Handlers: Execution Order
learnings.answer:
**Question:** given nested elements with click handlers, what's the output when clicking the inner one? Show the order under both bubbling and capturing. *The exact markup wasn't included, so here's the canonical three-level version — the reasoning transfers to any nesting.* ## The setup ```html
``` ```javascript const ids = ['grandparent', 'parent', 'child']; ids.forEach((id) => { const el = document.getElementById(id); el.addEventListener('click', () => console.log(`${id} — bubble`)); el.addEventListener('click', () => console.log(`${id} — capture`), true); }); ``` ## The output Clicking `#child`: ``` grandparent — capture parent — capture child — capture ← target phase; registration order decides child — bubble parent — bubble grandparent — bubble ``` **Bubbling only** (drop the `true` listeners): `child`, `parent`, `grandparent` — inside out. **Capturing only**: `grandparent`, `parent`, `child` — outside in. ## The part that catches people On the **target itself**, the capture flag is ignored. Both of `#child`'s listeners fire in the target phase, in the order they were added. That's why `child — capture` prints before `child — bubble` here — not because of the phase, but because it was registered first. Swap the two `addEventListener` lines and the order swaps. ## Stopping it ```javascript document.getElementById('parent').addEventListener('click', (e) => { e.stopPropagation(); console.log('parent — bubble (stopped here)'); }); ``` Now clicking the child logs the three captures, the child's bubble, `parent — bubble`, and **nothing from grandparent**. Call `stopPropagation()` in a *capturing* listener on `#grandparent` and the event never reaches the child at all — the click appears to do nothing. That's the overlay-blocking technique, and also a classic bug when a library does it to you. `stopImmediatePropagation()` goes further: it also prevents other listeners **on the same element** from running. ## Why this is asked It tests whether you know propagation is a *round trip* rather than a single upward pass, and whether you understand that `target` stays fixed while `currentTarget` changes. Both are load-bearing for [delegation](/learnings/152). ## Related - [Event Propagation: Bubbling, Capturing, and the Three Phases](/learnings/146) - [Event Delegation](/learnings/152) - [Event Bubbling vs Capturing](/learnings/28)
